title: Clarissa Littler - (roughly) a hundred days of poetry in partnership
speaker: Clarissa Littler
summary: Clarissa Littler describes a procedural generation project that generates the shapes of poems (line lengths in syllables, white space, meter, rhyme schemes) rather than the words, which she then fills in by writing poetry herself. She walks through a family of generators: random stanza blocks, sums of waves as line-length functions, 'signal functions' that place syllables and spaces within a line, metrical feet, and grab-bag rhyme assignment. Her argument is that a generator built as a creative partner has a low bar to be useful, because it only needs to push the human out of habitual forms, and that there is a sweet spot between freedom and over-constraint.

insights.claim: Littler's poetry generator produces the shape of a poem (form, layout, line structure, meter) rather than the words, so a human writes into a generated constraint.
insights.detail: She was stuck writing in similar voices and line shapes and wanted procgen to break her out of habits. The stated goal is not to generate poetry but to generate shapes of poetry, using the syllable as the base unit of English verse.
insights.quote: So the goal isn't to generate poetry. The goal is to generate shapes of poetry

insights.claim: Because poetry spans many forms, Littler built a family of generators starting from the simplest: stanzas of lines with randomly varied lengths around a mean.
insights.detail: The first generator just randomly sized stanzas and line lengths around a mean, displayed as dashes per syllable. She found it produced something in line with modern free verse but only a tiny sliver of what poetry can be.
insights.quote: we need not just one generator but a whole family of them

insights.claim: Summing randomly chosen waves into a function of line and stanza number gives line-length patterns that feel organic rather than either too regular or janky.
insights.detail: Littler generates line lengths as an arbitrary function of line and stanza number, built by adding pre-made wave pieces together. The result is smooth and varied without feeling artificially regular.
insights.quote: It is smooth, it's organic, it varies and yet it doesn't feel too regular or too artificially janky

insights.claim: Littler's 'signal functions' vary across a line, placing a syllable wherever the value is at or above zero and a space where it is below, to generate interleaved text and white space.
insights.detail: Generating indentation separately did not feel like modern poetry, which treats the page as an interleaving of text and white space. Using wave-based signal functions produced broken, deconstructed line shapes reminiscent of poets who tear apart classic line structure.
insights.quote: where they are greater equal to 0 that should be a syllable and where they are less than 0 that should be a space

insights.claim: Rhyme schemes can be generated by a grab bag: pick a number of rhyme endings proportional to poem length (at most about half the line count) and randomly assign them to lines.
insights.detail: This produces natural-looking schemes but can also produce oddities such as every line ending on the same sound. Littler embraced that weirdness and used slant rhymes to ease the monotony.
insights.quote: You don't want more than say half the number of lines of the poem to be different rhyming schemes

insights.claim: A generator meant as a creative partner has a low bar for usefulness because it only needs to make the human create differently, not mimic great work.
insights.detail: Littler says you can do a lot starting with very little because the goal is helping you write differently. As the generator gets weirder it pushes the writer to be weirder too, an iterative loop she calls the partnership.
insights.quote: What you are doing is trying to make something that helps you write poetry differently than you would and the threshold for that is actually not super high

insights.claim: Stacking too many generated constraints (stress patterns plus rhyme) makes creative work feel like puzzle-solving rather than expression.
insights.detail: Littler describes a sweet spot between freedom and constraint. Combining meter and rhyme felt over-constrained, a useful exercise but not something she would build publishable work from.
insights.quote: Stresses are rhyming starts to feel overconstrained. It is more like solving a puzzle than writing poetry
